speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In introducing this Bill some days ago I fully explained its purpose. Though it is a repeal of a statute of 1899 and its reenactment, this is done entirely for the purpose of. drafting, so that the Bill may be in good form. The actual change is very slight. Existing legislation provides that our banks doing business in colonies other than Canada shall have power to issue notes in those colonies. We have made provision for the issue of notes in pounds sterling and in Canadian dollars. But a case has arisen in which it is found that a bank which desired to issue notes in another colony discovered that its currency was slightly different from the currency of Canada. Although the currency of both countries is in dollars and cents, that slight difference is enough to prove an obstacle. The case arose in the colony of Trinidad, and the British government, through the colonial office, expressed the desire that the matter should be dealt with by legislation in the parliament of Canada. What we propose therefore is that a bank doing business in any British colony shall have a right to issue its notes in that colony in the currency of the colony in actual commercial use. That is the whole matter. There are only a few words changed in the Act.
Is there any provision in the Bill as to what proportion of the circulation is outside of Canada ? That might perhaps be of importance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have never required it. But of course under the general provision calling for a special return, we can obtain it at any time. Perhaps my hon. friend is right in the suggestion, it might be desirable information ; but the Bank Act gives power to obtain it by calling for a special return.
When the minister spoke before I asked if these notes would be legal tender in the Dominion. We give them authority to issue the notes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, they would not be legal tender in Canada. In fact, except under special conditions, a bank note is not a legal tender. Here we provide simply that the notes shall be redeemed in the colony in which they are issued, so long as the bank does business in that colony ; but if for any reason business is suspended, then they must be redeemed in Canada. The idea is that the circulation of the notes shall be confined to the colony in question because, as they represent a different currency, it would be rather confusing to have their notes circulated in Canada. They are not a legal tender.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair, there is a matter which I wish to call to the attention of the government in connection with the public wharf at Campbellton, Restigouche county, N.B. It seems that there is just one public wharf at Campbellton, which all the shippers of lumber, particularly at that port, are obliged to use, but it seems that one corporation have been granted a preference in the use of this wharf by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, without any good reason therefor. The wharf is necessary for the economical shipment of lumber at that port. An order was given, a copy of which I have, and which I will read, by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, dated .Tune 1C, 1904, addressed to Mr. Asker, who is the wharfinger at Campbellton. Tt is as follows :
Sir,-I am to instruct you to see that ships taking cargo direct from the cars on the government wharf at Campbellton are given the railway or wharf berth. It has, the department understands, been the custom in the past for the first vessel in to get the choice of berths but in future precedence is to be given in this connection to vessels loading from the cars.
I am, sir, your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) F. GOURDEAU, Deputy Minister M. and F. To Mr. G. E. Asker,
Wharfinger, Campbellton, N.B.
As a matter of fact at this government wharf there is only room for one steamer to load at a time, and the complaint is made that the corporation known as the Shives Lumber Company have the right under this order, which is given here, to take the wharf and to take this berth whenever they choose, no matter whether other vessels are in before them or not. Complaint was made to the department in a letter written by the William Richards Company, Limited, under date of June 23, 1904. That letter is as follows :
Campbellton, N.B., June 23, 1904.
F. Gourdeau, Esq.,

and F.,
Ottawa, Can.
Dear Sir,-In reference to inclosed copy of your instruction of June 16 to Mr. Asker, war-finger at this port, we hardly think that you know or are at all aware of the condition of affairs at this port or you would not have issued the order in question. We will, as briefly as possible, give you the condition of affairs. At the port of Campbellton there are only two shippers that have been shipping deals over the government wharf, they being the Shives Lumber Co. (Limited) and ourselves, and in fact up to this year have been the only ship-

pers from this port in recent years. We, as a rule, load the bulk of our cargoes from lighters, *while the Shives Company' load theirs from cars and lighters, but this year they will load the most from Cars, whereas we will load none from cars, and they shall have full charge of this government wharf under this order. As far as the order is concerned, the wharf is the only berth where steamers can load with safety, and if the Shives Lumber Company are given the full control of this wharf it means that our company have to carry deals on lighters to Point le Garde, some ten miles below Camp-bellton, which is the only safe berth for a steamer to load within the port of Campbell-ton, excepting the government wharf. If such a state of affairs continues it means that this company, in order to do business, must do such business at a great loss to themselves, as well as doing injury to the port, as there is no safe berth within the port, and there are days when you cannot load a steamer at Point le Garde, because it is an open and exposed roadway, and lighters cannot put alongside the ship. We feel that if this order is carried out as intended, and we have no rights to the use of the government property at this port, and it is given over to one shipper for their absolute use and benefit, it means that we cannot see any course left open to us but to stop doing business and shipping from this port. We might further add that we have a very valuable plant situated at this port and are large employers of labour and make more use of the wharf than any other shippers, as by reference to the customs here you will ascertain. We would therefore ask that the said order be cancelled forthwith and that both shippers be given equal rights in regard to the use of government, whai'fs and property at this port and that the old state of affairs be restored, namely, that the first vessel arriving to have the preference of the use of the government wharfs on payment of the proper tolls, and we would thank you to give this matter your serious and prompt consideration, as we can asure you that it is a very serious matter as far as this port is concerned. Awaiting your reply.
We are, your respectfully,
(Sgd.) WM. RICHARDS & CO. (Ltd.)
To that letter the department replied by the following letter bearing date of July 2nd, and addressed to Win. Richards & Company, Limited :
Your letter of the 23rd of June has been fully considered. Instructions were given Mr. Asker, wharfinger, to give the preference to vessels loading from the cars. It was understood that Mr. Shives, at considerable expense, placed a siding on the wharf in order that vessels might be loaded from the cars.
I am instructed that that is absolutely untrue ; I am instructed that Mr. Shives did nothing of the sort ; I am instructed that Mr. Shives expended no money upon the government wharf after the expropriation proceedings were taken.
In view of the fact and the expense to which Mr. Shives has been put

Remember, this is the sole ground upon which this preference is granted according to the letter of the department.
In view of the fact and the expense to which Mr. Shives has been put, it seems reasonable that vessels that have been loaded from the cars should be given the preference with regard to the berth. It was also understood that two vessels being there together owned by different firms would rarely occur, and consequently any other firm shipping lumber would not to any extent suffer. The department does not wish to place any obstacle in the way of yourselves in loading lumber from the wharf, and would be pleased to consider your interest as well as that of Mr. Shives. It is understood that there will be a large expenditure for wharf accommodation at your wharf in the future, and that there will be abundance of room for lumber dealers to load and unload lumber in Campbellton.
That is a case of : live horse and you'll get grass.
In the meantime, I do not consider that the instructions to Mr. Asker can be at this stage cancelled unless you are able to prove that you are suffering severe damage.
In reply to that, the .Messrs. Richards and Company addressed another letter dated 6th July in which they say :
Re inclosed correspondence, we would like to add that since this order has been issued and it has become known, it has already compelled us to pay extra freight over the other shipper from this port, as the steamship owners are fully aware that when a steamer moves to Point le Garde, that it involves a lot of extra expense; we might say that we have recently had to pay 5 per standard on account of this order, and think that in all decencv and fair-play it should be cancelled.
This means, that if Richards and Company cannot have the use of the government wharf they must load their steamers at Point le Garde which is ten miles distant, and in an open roadway which in storms from certain quarters is very dangerous for steamers. It is impossible to carry on the loading there under certain conditions. The steamer is detained therefore much longer than would be necessary, if she were at the government wharf and in consequence Richards and Company have to pay higher rates on the shipments of deals. The letter continues :
We also have a steamer in port since last Friday, and on Saturday the writer requested the harbour master to allow him to have the berth after the Shives steamer ' sailed, and the reply he got was this, that Mr. Shives had a sailing vessel, that he wanted to load at the wharf, and if he wanted the steamer to get the berth we woould have to arrange with Mr. Shives. Our steamer is some 1,600 tons and is loading from lighters in the stream, and the Shives barque is only 800 tons and loading from lighters in the stream, and wo are informed that most of her cargo is coming in lighters. The barque could load safely where she is. as she is only geting 35 M. of dry boards per day and our steamer is loading at the rate of 200 M. per day, and if she does not. get the berth as soon as vacated by the Shi-ves steamer on Friday will have to proceed to Point le Garde to take in balance of

her cargo, which will likely be one million. At present there are In port one steamer and one large sailing ship for us and one steamer and one sailing ship for Shives, as well as a number of schooners that cannot get a berth at all. You will see at once that our claim is fair and just, and we cannot see how the government or department can give over public property like this to one concern and debar the rest of the public. We trust that the department will at once cancel this order or it will be not only very injurious to ourselves, but to the port and public in general.
It seems that the Shives Company hail a wharf alongside the government wharf, and that in order to reach the government wharf it was necessary to cross the Shives wharf. Expropriation proceedings were taken by the government to get the Shives wharf ; the government offered Mr. Shives, or the corporation of which he is the head, some $5,000 for the wharf, but $40,000 or $50,000 was demanded, and the award of the arbitrators was $35,000. which I understand the government has appealed, and it is now before the Exchequer Court. But it does not appear from anything on the face of this correspondence or from any other evidence, that the Shives Company has any right to any preference. The point is made that the Shives Company is loading lumber from the cars, but I fail to see how that could give them a preference on this government wharf over other shippers. I am informed that the allegation that any expenditure has been made by Mr. Shives for a siding on this wharf is absolutely untrue.- Anyway, what right would Mr. .Shives have to run a railway track upon the government wharf ? It seems to me that whoever is in charge of that public wharf would be derelict in their duty if they allowed any private individual or corporation to make such use of government property. In view of the strong statements made in this letter and in view of all the circumstances, it seems to me that this order-a very improper order in the first place-should be cancelled, and that fair play and equal rights, what we call British justice should be meted out to each man who desires to use that wharf-and who is willing to pay tolls for that use.

Surely the hou. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) does not expect me to give him the information without any notice whatever being given in advance. If the hon. gentleman had wanted the information to-day, he should have certainly given me notice last night or yesterday. I know nothing whatever about this matter, but will make the necessary inquiry and bring down the information.

I mentioned this matter yesterday in supply, and I stated that I would bring it up again at the first opportunity. I would suppose that was sufficient notice. I did not intend to be guilty of any discourtesy in not giving notice.

EMMERSON (Minister of Railways and Canals.) My attention has not been called to this matter, but as the question of a railway siding is involved I wish to say that there was an appropriation last year for laying rails and ties on a siding connecting the new industry at Camp-bellton established by the Shives Lumber Company, with the Intercolonial railway. The Shives Company graded the siding and we put down the rails and ties with the view of securing to the Intercolonial railway the products of that mill, which they would ship by water if this were not done. The products of the mill are brought down over the Intercolonial railway and shipped from the public wharf at Campbellton. An extension of that wharf is arranged for whereby a turntable will be used, and I have no doubt that within a very short time provision will be made for more vessels than one. That of course will be done at the expense of the Intercolonial railway, in order that it may have the advantage of the traffic, and not at the expense of any individual or corporation. Do I understand the Richards Company lighter their material to the wharf and then load it from the lighters, or do they haul it on to the wharf and have it shipped ?
I do not know, but I presume the latter.
Their mill is on the line of the Intercolonial railway, but I do not know whether they utilize the railway or whether they haul their lumber.
They do both. Sometimes they haul by the railway and sometimes they carry by lighter.

Mr. R, L. BORDEN. Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair I would like to inquire of the government whether or not they have any further information as to the date on which the report of the commission appointed to investigate certain matters in the Yukon will be laid on the table of the House. So far as I am aware, it has not been laid on the table up to the present time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Does my hon. friend refer to. the report of Mr. Justice Britton ?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, it has not been laid on the table yet.

There seems to be an extraordinary delay in this matter. The instructions to the commission were issued in June of last year, some thirteen months ago. The commission had not a wide scope, although a promise was made by the member for the Yukon in the election campaign that certain ' charges of fraud would be investigated as soon as par-

Jiament met. The hon. gentleman's health was not such as to enable him to be present till some time after parliament met. I am not saying that in reproach to him ; but in his address to the electors of the Yukon there was a promise made that charges of fraud would be thoroughly investigated. That promise was ratified last year by the Postmaster General, when the matter was first brought up by the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. T. Chase Casgrain). I do not propose to go over the discussion which we had last year on the instructions to the commission which were brought down by the government-instrue tions which did not admit of the investigation of the circumstances attending the granting of the concessions. We on this side of the House demanded that wider powers should be given, so that all those circumstances should be investigated by the commissioners. Although that investigation had clearly been promised by the Postmaster General, the promise was afterwards withdrawn ; and the instructions to the commissioners were carefully framed so that no such inquiry could be made. The inquiry, such as it was, proceeded before two commissioners- Mr. Justice Britton, of the bench of Ontario, and Mr. Bell. The inquiry, so far as it went, was concluded, and from that time to the present we have had no report ; although, if I remember rightly, the inquiry was concluded in November or December last. This House has now been in session nearly five months, and it was not unreasonable for us to expect long before this that the report of Mr. Justice Britton should have been received. I do not know whether any report, or any draft report, from the other commissioner, who met his death by a deplorable accident, was ever received by the government. It is well known that Mr. Bell stated before his death that his report had been drafted. No trace of it has ever been found, and I assume that no copy of it, certainly not the original, has come into the hands of the government. If it was ever received, its nonproduction merits the severest criticism. Its disappearance has undoubtedly been very mysterious, because I believe no trace of it has been round among Mr. Bell's papers. Since Mr. Bell's death the matter has been before Mr. Justice Britton, and I should have thought he could have made up his report ten times during the period at his disposal. I am saying that with all respect to the necessity of his performing his judicial duties ; because, if his judicial duties are of such a character that he has been unable during the seven or eight months which have elapsed sUnce the investigation was closed, to prepare his report to parliament on this subject, then he should never have been appointed on this commission. The whole inquiry has been absolutely farcical. It was farcical, to begin with, because that which had been promised to the people of the Yukon during the elec-
'tion campaign by my hon. friend who represents that constituency was not granted. It has been farcical, in the next place, because seven or eight months have elapsed since the investigation was completed, and apparently parliament is to be prorogued without having an opportunity to consider that report. I desire to place on record my protest against this method of conducting the public business. There was a very unanimous cry-not a party cry, but a cry from one end of the Yukon to the other-to have, not only the investigation which the government has given, but an investigation of a very much wider character. The limited investigation that was given, was given thirteen months ago, and from that time to this we have not heat'd one word of what that investigation amounted to, or what the opinion of the commissioners was. I do not think the government are to be congratulated on the way in which they have dealt with this subject, and I conclude by once more asking the Prime Minister whether or not we are to have, even in the closing days of this session, any report from Mr. Justice Britton ?

Mr. Speaker, I think I can fairly say that the matter which my hon. friend has brought to the attention of the House is no longer an issue, and has been disposed of more than once on the floor of this House. It is quite true, promises were made at one time by parties who were not in the government, but who spoke in the interest of common justice, that certain charges of fraud, which were made in the Yukon, would be investigated. The government expressed its willingness to have such an investigation when particulars were given ; but we refused to authorize a blanket investigation into charges Which were not formulated. Such being the intention of the government, expressed more than once in this House, a commission was issued last year to Mr. Justice Britton and Mr. Bell authorizing them to investigate, not the charges of fraud which had been made, but the nature of the concession, the needs of the Yukon, and especially the wants of the miners as to water. The death of Mr. Bell was most disastrous in many respects. It is stated that his report was drafted. That may be, but, so far as I know, the draft never reached the government. In the absence of the Minister of the Interior, I would not say any more. With regard to the report of Mr. Justice Britton, I do not know that he has made his report as yet. He has been communicated with once more to hasten it, so that we may have it before the House rises. I may say that the necessity which existed at one time for this investigation has been removed by the fact that the Treadgold concession, which most of the complaints had reference to, is no longer in existence.

It seems to me that the very fact that the Treadgold people have abandoned their privileges is all the more reason why this matter should be investigated. It will be within the recollection of hon. members that members of the House were sent again and again copies of newspapers which support the government from the Yukon making the most serious and damaging allegations. Public opinion seemed to have been aroused at the enormity of the transaction ; and the commission having been appointed, it seems most unfair, notwithstanding its limited power, that parliament should be prorogued without having the report of Mr. Justice Britton. It is seven or eight months since the commission ceased taking evidence, and Mr. Justice Britton has either had time or has not had time to make his report. I understand that he has been in Ottawa several times during the last three or four months. Has the government received any information from him as to what progress he has made with his report ? I understand that no report has been received by the government from the late Mr. Bell. Has the government received any information as to the progress of this report, and is there any possibility of our having it before prorogation ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot say off-hand whether that is possible or not, but will inquire.

That seems an extraordinary reply, in view of what has taken place recently. The Treadgold concession has been cancelled by the government because no doubt of some information conveyed to it through some channel that it would be improper to continue it or carry it out. That is the only conclusion which we can reach. Through what channel did that information come ? The government have their own channel, and were inquiring into the charges made with reference to that concession. The charges were of a most specific character. They were not made by opponents of the government, but by their own friends. Letter after letter is in the possession of members on this side, written by friends of the government, complaining that they had made every representation possible, and could get no redress. These friends of the government complain that they elected a representative to this House, who became dumb from the day he entered it up to the present, because, so far as they knew, he has never opened his mouth in this House to bring to the notice of the administration the complaints which people were making, and the difficulties under which they were labouring.
He ran away.

The government promised to have a full investigation, and the member elected promised his constituents to have an investigation made as soon as Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
he reached parliament. That member has been in parliament a long time, and if such an investigation were made what information has reached the government as the result of it. We are utterly in the dark regarding what took place. It is true that one of the commissioners is dead, but the other is still living. Can it be possible that he is so busily engaged in his different duties that he is unable to make a report ? He was appointed to inquire and report, so as to put parliament in possession of the information which parliament ought to have in order to deal intelligently with the question, yet during the whole of this session, which has lasted nearly five months, this commissioner has given up most of his time to his ordinary duties, and has so far made no report to parliament. That is treating parliament with contempt. It is not treating parliament with that courtesy to which it is entitled from its own officials, and this commissioner is really an official of this parliament. It is treating the representatives of the people with contempt. It is treating the people of that country, who have made complaints regarding the condition of affairs, with great contempt. I have in my possession a letter describing the kind of inquiry which was made. I do not know the gentleman who writes the letter, but ho is represented to me as an intelligent, respectable, law-abiding citizen. He says that the inquiry was a perfect farce, that he was called down by the commissioner several times for doing what his counsel advised liim he had a perfect right to do. He endeavoured to place information before that commission, but the commission refused to receive it or allow him to give it and would only receive just such information as the commissioners asked for. Following that procedure, an indictment was made against him and he was told that if he did not conduct himself better he would be dealt with for contempt of court.
Dragooned.

Yes, dragooned for contempt of court. His answer to this threat was that he did not see how it was possible for any one to have greater contempt for the court than he had in view of the way in which he had been treated. But; out of that grew some other trouble for which he was put in prison; and as far as I know, he has been lying in prison ever since. He was refused the common justice of being judged by his own peers. He was refused a jury trial. He was deliberately thrown into prison, and is there yet. He writes to know if anything can be done, and if that commission has reported. He was indicted on another charge which, I believe, arose out of this matter before the commission-the charge of taking logs which he thought he had a perfect right to take. He was denied trial by jury, and tried by a stipendiary magistrate, and is now in prison.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Do I understand tlie lion, gentleman to say that some one was thrown Into prison by order of the commissioner for contempt of court ?
Not by order of the commissioner ; but he was Indicted before a stipendiary magistrate, and thrown into prison, and Is there yet.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That happens everywhere.

If that kind of inquiry is enough to satisfy the government, it is not enough to satisfy the people out there. If that kind of justice satisfies the government, it is not what will satisfy lovers of British justice in any part of the British empire. It is a high-handed proceeding, which is devoid of the essence of fair play or justice. These things require to be ventilated, and the only opportunity we have is to discuss them in parliament, and to do that properly we should have the report before us. We are now in the closing days of the session, and we want to know whether it is the intention of the government to lay that report on the table, and give us an opportunity of considering it. Is the government going to content itself with the cancelling of the Treadgold concession ? What is the reason that the government does not dare to bring down that report, or give parliament the reasons why it has cancelled the Treadgold concession ? Parliament is entitled to know why. On what information has the government acted ? That information should be given parliament, and above all things the commission appointed | over a year ago ought to have had its work done long ago' and reported to parliament, so that we might deal with this question in the light of all the information available.

Has any communication been had with Mr. Justice Britton regarding this report ? The right lion, gentleman will perceive the pertinency of this question when he remembers what took place in the Senate a few days ago. The government has declared that the Secretary of State was not warranted in the statement he then made that the remaining commissioner would not report. Has Mr. Justice Britton been requested to make a report ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I can inform my hon. friend that Mr. Justice Britton has been communicated with.
What is his reply ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is more than I can say at present. The Secretary of State made a statement some time ago in the Senate, to which attention was called, and he then communicated with Mr. Justice Britton, and instructed him to take his letter as not written, and hasten his report.

BENNETT The other day, when the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce were being discussed,
I brought up what is known as the Jackson matter in the province of Ontario, namely, the appointment of Mr J. B. Jackson, formerly of Ingersoll, to the position of commercial agent in Leeds, England. The minister stated that when an item was reached under the heading of commercial agencies, the matter might be taken up. As the hon. minister saw fit to discontinue his estimates, no opportunity to discuss it was reached, and I am bringing it up now.
Some few years ago a general election was held in the province of Ontario, and as the result of the death of one of the elected members, the Ross government found itself with a majority of only one. All the sacrifices which had been used in Ontario for many years had been resorted to, and then the government, staggering under what was a decisive defeat, saw that something had to be done. Their only hope was to resort to the courts. After looking over the field they seized on South Oxford which had for many years been a Liberal stronghold and they thought if they could succeed in unseating the Conservative candidate there they could win that riding. A close study of the whole situation revealed the fact that they could not by legitimate means unseat Donald Sutherland, the Conservative member, who had been returned by a majority of about 150. There lived in the town of Ingersoll in the county of Oxford J. B. Jackson, a particular friend of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, a gentleman whose name has figured very conspicuously' in those hand to hand encounters which have signalized the entrance of the Minister of Trade and Commerce into the party conventions of that riding, and there can be no doubt that of all the men who have done yeoman service for the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the bitter, acrimonious fights to secure the nomination, none stood closer to the minister than did Mr. Jackson. It was notorious in Woodstock, Ingersoll and all that neighbourhood that Jackson was carrying in his pocket the appointment of county judge of the county of Huron. That was life and well known there. This and other offices had been promised to Jackson and I can only produce in substantiation of that, Jackson's own sworn testimony. He was asked referring to certain offices which had been mentioned, and said :
Well there are several in my mind and have been for several years.
And being asked if several positions had been the subject of discussion, he replied :
Well, I do not know that.
He was asked :

Will you swear to that, that have been mentioned between yourself and those in whose gifts these officers are ?
He replied :
Oh, I suppose that conversations have taken place between me and others in regard to that in the last few years.
So it is quite clear from the statement in evidence of Jackson that he expected something from this government. It is clear that the Minister of Trade and Commerce was solely responsible for this man's appointment because the Minister of Public Works speaking at Woodstock when complaint was made as to Jackson's appointment said :
I have heard since I came home something in reference to acts of Mr. Jackson that were not creditable to him ; but his appointment was a departmental matter, under the minister, Sir Richard Cartwright, and I have no doubt that he had no idea there was anything wrong.
This statement was made by Hon. Mr. Sutherland last winter and it cannot be expected that the public will be so gullible as to believe that a man of the ability of the Minister of Trade and Commerce had not heard of the peculiar and improper acts of Jackson as commented upon at the time. It is true that Hon. Mr. Sutherland here refers to some improper acts. I do not know that he means, because he does not say specifically, Jackson's action in connection with this trial. He may refer to some other actions that were dismissed in that neighbourhood. There was a prosecution of this same Jackson on a charge of forgery before the courts of Oxford which was dismissed owing to the fact that in some mysterious manner the very document that was the basis of the charge disappeared. I shall not refer to other charges that are rife there, but I assume and it is fair to assume that what Hon. Mr. Sutherland referred to as improper acts on the part of Jackson are those acts which were condemned and rightly condemned by one of the trial judges.
I have before me the evidence in this case as heard before Mr. Justice Britton and Mr. Justice Street when after days of fishing and days long drawn out of evidence given, the court had only two cases before them and on these two cases, most trival in their nature, one judge was in favour of acquittal and the other in favour of unseating. An appeal was taken to the court of aippeal, but the appeal court decided that an appeal did not lie where two judges disagreed in that manner and Mr. Sutherland was sustained in his seat. I shall not advert to the judgment which Mr. Justice Britton gave, but it was an unfortunate thing for that judge coming fresh from politics wherein no one wall say that he had not been a bitter partisan, that on two most trifling charges that were backed up by evidence of a scatly character Judge Britton should have decided against Mr. Sutherland while

Judge Street decided in his favour. Be that as it may Mr. Donald Sutherland was sustained and I am going to refer to the facts which led up to the prosecution or persecution of Mr. Donald Sutherland. There have been many election trials in this Dominion but no other trial can be compared to this one. Jackson was the solicitor in the case, living in Ingersoll, right in the centre of that well populated riding. He was conversant with all the adjacent towns. He had carte blanche and unlimited funds to find evidence, whether true or false, as sworn to by witnesses, to unseat Sutherland.
Now what is some of the evidence that proves that I have here the sworn evidence of this Mr. Jackson ? Jackson goes through that riding and one approach that he makes is to Mr. Chambers in Woodstock. I need not give a verbatim account of the evidence but briefly it is this : He approached Chambers in Woodstock, a man whom he had practically not known up to that time, goes into his place of business, addresses him in a familiar way and after serving him with the subpoena says :	We will require you
at the trial. He then invites him across the street to have a cigar. As soon as they reach the hotel he asks Chambers to adjourn to a private room and once there starts at Chambers with a most astonishing proposition. He says that he is prepared to spend an almost unlimited amount of money in order that evidence may be secured against Sutherland and his agents in order to effect his downfall. Chambers mentions $5,000 and, after a little parley, it is arranged that this man Jackson shall come from his own home in Ingersoll to Woodstock and at the house of Chambers discuss the terms upon which Chambers shall produce evidence, whether true or false, that will bring about the defeat of Sutherland on the protest and his consequent unseating. Chambers was a man of prominence in the community and he at once went to certain friends of his and divulged the whole affair. The result was that, true to his promise, Jackson turned up at Woodstock on a subsequent evening. On this occasion Chambers had taken the precaution to have two responsible gentlemen conveniently situated where they could'overhear what was said during the interview. Chambers was not going to trust himself to the tender mercies of Jackson, for prior to this time Jackson had a most unsavoury reputation. These two gentlemen heard everything. Jackson's proposition as admitted in his own sworn evidence was that he would pay $375 to Chambers if evidence was forthcoming, perjured or true, and $375 more should be furnished to Chambers if eight charges were proven. They go on further and discuss it and Jackson further makes this offer that if the charges were successfully proven $1,500 might be paid to Chambers. It was necessary in order to get evidence to resort to

witnesses who knew nothing whatever of the matter, but who could be suborned to perjure themselves. Chambers had furnished certain names of men as Chambers was right in the game. He knew nothing of any improper wrong doing and consequently Jackson did not call any of these men into the box because he found subsequently' that he had been hoaxed and had been deprived of $375.
But Jackson turns in another direction, and that seems to have been a very fertile field in the riding of South Oxford, namely, to resort to the most abandoned characters, men who were proved by' the records of the police court to have been time and again arrested on criminal charges. One man who is a strong witness against Sutherland on the personal charge, had served a term in the Central Prison at Toronto. What is some of the evidence of this man ? A man named Charles Parker testified that a brother-in-law of his, named George Fournier, came to him and asked him if he would swear that he got money from a man named Joseph Clark ; and he was given the further option that if he did not want to swear that he got the money from Clark he could swear that he got it from a man named Sindon, and if he did'nt want to swear that he got it from him he could swear that he got it from a man named Davis. He was offered the option of three different men from whom he could swear that he got the money. There looms up then from the office of Kerr, Macdonald & Grant, Toronto, who seem to be engaged in all these election protests, a fellow named Sullivan or Sutherland, who is notorious as a part of the machine in the province of Ontario. This Sutherland had been celebrated in a certain provincial election trial in the county of Lennox, and Sutherland makes the further admission that he went to this man and swore it on Sindon or Johnson, or a third man whose name I forget. Now the house will wonder why he was given the option of three men to swear it on. The reason was this, that Clark was a coloured man, and everybody knows there is a certain amount of prejudice against men of colour. Therefore it was decided by this foxy Sutherland, after a good deal of consultation with Jackson and the rest of the gang, that this charge was to be put on this man Clark. But it would not be well to have Clark go into the box and swear that he had received a sum of money from some reputable man in the town of Oxford -because this took place in the county of Oxford ; and in that case it would be necessary to swear that it was got from some man whose word would not avail him, and something more than that was necessary to have the other parties opportunely turn up and he able to swear that they heard the conversation. So he got Fournier to promise that he would be on hand and would swear the story true. He also says
another man named Keir is to be on hand in order to corroborate the story. Now Fournier swears that he had conversations with Jackson, repeated conversations in Jackson's office, and although we are not able to prove that Fournier and Jackson were in combination, because neither of the two will admit that they tried to bribe this man Parker, still we do know that Jackson admits that he paid $5 to Fournier himself, that he paid $5 to Parker himself, although Parker says he got $10 from Jackson. Then he was to swear that the coloured man had paid him $5. Then Parker meets again this man Sutherland in Jackson's office, and there he is promised by Sutherland that he will be paid $20, and in the event of his losing his position in. the city hospital where he was employed, he would secure him a position on the government canal. Now if the story of this man Parker were not true, it would have been fair for them to have called Sutherland, and to have denied the statement made by him.	But	Sutherland although a short time prior to that was in the city of Woodstock, could not be found, and Sutherland's solicitors were unable to find him and put him in the box either to corroborate or deny the statement of Parker. Then there was another man who figured prominently, one named Anderson, county constable in the town of Tilsonburg. Then a man named Fick was given by Jackson a considerable sum of money, some $250, and he employed himself in going about the country and attempting subornation or perjury, and witness testified that he received money from Fick, and yet when the trial comes on Fick, also flies from the country and cannot be found. The result was that they could get no denial from Fick and no corroboration of the witnesses called by Sutherland. Then they called a man named Frederick Avey and he testifies :
One Hewlett cancelled store account of $40 for signing a declaration. Jackson told me to say nil as to the account. Jackson came to my house at Norwich.
Now -the game followed out was this : Prior to holding the trial these men Sutherland, Jackson, Fick, Wright and Hewlett would go to these abandoned characters in the police court and get declarations from them that they had received certain sums of money, and then they would afterwards be able to confront these men with the declarations and say : You made this solemn declaration, now we expect you to swear it through. In the case of this fellow Hewlett who cancelled the $40 store account, he will swear that he received from a Conservative a certain amount of money. Jackson acknowledges himself the fellow who went to his house at Norwich, and Jackson further asks him to say nothing as to the account, to say nothing as to having got the

$40 for making this declaration, and which declaration Avery replies was untrue. Another man named Pollard says :
Hewlett paid me $25 for declaration. I was promised $75 and protection from law. Jackson saw me at Norwich and told me to say nil about the declaration.
That is what is guaranteed in the province of Ontario to those who give testimony in election trials where wrong doing has been committed, namely immunity from prosecution by law. The same thing was done in the West Elgin trial, and in all these trials in the province of Ontario men who have been wrong-doers have never been brought to book, everything has been covered up. No wonder that this man Pollard, when he was sure of protection against the law, and that the Attorney General of Ontario would not prosecute him said he believed the statements made by Hewlett,. Then a man named W. A. Young is called and he says :
Sutherland of Kerr's office told me he would give me $25 if I would stick to charge on respondent.
So it goes all through the evidence. Witness after witness is called who testify that they received money for making those declarations, and then afterwards when they were brought to book in court, openly admitted that they knew nothing at all as to the truth of these charges, that they were false, that they had not been paid this money for making the declarations. Now it cannot be argued that Jackson did not know who these men were. They were all living not far from each other, and they came into contact several times with the solicitor of the government. He must have been making inquiries. What is Fournier's record :
Convicted August 12, 1901 of being drunk and disorderly, fined $5 and costs. Convicted 22nd January, 1898 of assault, fined $1 and costs. Convicted 8th June, 1894 of assault and battery, fined $1 and costs. Tried July 17, 1896 on a charge of perjury, dismissed on a technicality as explained in the evidence of Mayor Sinclair.
Another man named Keilor, who was one of the corroborative witnesses, had been committed to three months in jail for vagrancy. Another man named Mustard was convicted of theft and again of being drunk and disorderly. A man named Collins, who swore a charge on Mr. King of Ingersoll. was convicted of an indecent assault and fined $50 and costs. Again convicted of being drunk and disorderly, again drunk and disorderly, convicted on three different charges of theft and sentenced to four years in Kingston penitentiary ; charged by his wife with attempting to commit suicide. A large number of witnesses swore his reputation was so bad that they could not believe him on oath.

Then there was John Henderson who swore this charge on Johnson in corroboration with Parker. Henderson was convicted of being drunk and disorderly ; again convicted of breaking and entering a shop of John Christophers and stealing goods therefrom, sentenced to 18 months in the Central Prison. Isaiah Wright, who swore to charge on Johnson, was convicted on October 15, 1890, of being drunk and disorderly, sentenced to 30 days in jail ; again convicted of larceny, sentenced to 365 days in the Central Prison ; another charge of drunk and disorderly, 30 days ; convicted of assault, $1 and costs ; another charge of drunk and disorderly, 30 days ; another charge of drunk and disorderly, 10 days; another charge of drunk and disorderly, 20 days; another charge of drunk and disorderly, 20 days ; convicted of theft, 3 months in common jail ; disturbance, 6 months in Central Prison ; non-support, 6 months in Central Prison ; theft, 29 days in Central prison ; drunk, $1 and costs ; drunk and incapable, $2 and costs ; drunk and disorderly, 30 days in common jail ; drunk, $1 and costs. And these are the men who are the confidants, friends and accomplices of this Canadian representative in Leeds today. But what was the whole condition of this matter ? It is all very well to make comments here but we have the comments that a gentleman made, who was right under the guns, so to speak, who was holding the inquiry into the fact. When this matter was before the court and when man after man had been placed in the box, the comment of Mr. Justice Street, as reported in the ' Globe' of October 20, 1902, was as follows :
Judge Street interposed saying : ' Mr. Blake was quite within his rights in calling attention to the means that have been taken to procure evidence in this case. One of the difficulties I have in this case is the knowledge of the improper and reprehensible means and large expenditure which have been proven to have been devoted to an absolutely improper purpose. It, is impossible to follow' the ramifications of such an expenditure, and in dealing with the last case I cannot get out of my mind the possibility of the course of the inquiry having been affected by the expenditure of a very large sum.of money. Here is Mr. Jackson, a lawyer in Ingersoll, here is this man of the lowest possible character, as far as appears from what has been said about him, and one knows of the desperate efforts that have been made to prove the charges. Nothing was ever heard in my experience before like it. It is impossible to trace out all these underground influences.
And yet this is a sample of the men who to-day are to be found in Great Britain as the representatives of this country. Mr. W. T. R. Preston certainly had an unsavoury reputation in this country, but even Ms reputation is as the rose compared with that of this man Jackson. How did Jackson act when he was in the box ? There is no doubt 1 that Jackson was trying to save himself as

much as he could. When he was driven from pillar to post, he was forced to admit that he had never kept any record of these moneys that he had been paying out. He had paid Chambers 8375. Fick 8250, and a considerable amount to Hewlett as well as paying all these other individuals one after another as they came into his office, different small amounts. What does he say ?
Q. And have you got no book in which you have entered that ?
A. I have not.
Q. How do you keep track of such payments ?
A. Well, I sometimes paid by cheque but I generally tried to keep track of such payments.
Q. In what way, I am asking you ?
A. Well, in my mind.
Q. In your mind ?
A. Yes.
Q. Are all your cash transactions done in the
same way ?
A. Not my business transactions.
Q. This you did not call a business transaction ?
A. Well, I was paying him and I think I gave him about $150 and about $100 besides to pay for subpoenaing some 46 witnesses.
Then he was referring to Fick :
I was not asking you that ; you told me you paid him $150 and now you tell me you paid him another $100, that is- $250. I asked you what track you kept of it and have you any entry in any book of that ?
A. I have not any entry in any hook of that.
What does all that show ? It shows that Jackson knew that he was being involved in a discreditable and disgraceful proceeding. What is going to be the end of this sort of thing if it is to go on in this country 7 It would seem that Jackson was supplied with funds to an unlimited extent and there is no statement on his part that this was his own money. It is incredible to think that this was his own money. Chambers in his statement says that Jackson told him that he was going to Toronto to see some members of the government and I think he said Mr. Ross amongst them, although I will not say as to that, and that when he did come back he did see him about it, and all the information that we have about Jackson's circumstances is decidedly of the nature that would go to show, that $375 was not an amount of money to be found every day on the person of Jackson. Then it must be positively the fact that this money was furnished from headquarters. I am not going to say that Mr. Ross, or whoever supplied him with the money, was aware of the purpose for which it was to be used, but here is the money on Jackson who was able to secure command of this money and here is the conclusion of the judge after hearing the evidence, who says, that the conduct of Jackson was in every way most disgraceful and discreditable. Two charges were brought against the respondent Sutherland.
one a question of disqualification-for giving an hostler a fifty cent tip, and these were the subject of a disagreement between the judges. Men were found to give the evidence and accomplices turned up to corroborate fheir statements. The plan was so laid that there was always corroborative evidence. In face of the fact that this matter was commented on publicly at the time in the newspapers it is idle for the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commehce to say that he never heard of it. It would; be incredible on the part of any reasonable person to believe that the right hon. gentleman never heard of the South Oxford election trial. He must have read these comments of the judges. As a party man, he was interested in the South Oxford riding. As to the success or failure of his party in South Oxford whether in federal or local affairs it goes without saying that he would be interested. He has been the representative of South Oxford for a great many years in this House, and there is no reasonable man who will ever be got to believe for a moment that the right hon. gentleman did not read the comments of the judges on the evidence adduced at the trial. So that, at the time of the appointment of this man Jackson, it is impossible for us to believe that he was not aware of his wrong doing cn that occasion. As to the matter of the appointment we must not forget that the hon. Minister of Public Works has declared that the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce is solely responsible for the appointment and employment of this man Jackson, and I think the right hon. gentleman owes it to the country and to the House to explain why Jackson in the first instance was ever secured by the government to perform the duties of the office that he now fills and in the next place why, in face of the allegations that have been made against this man in the House and in the face of the means that the right hon. gentleman has had of gaining access to the records which will prove the truth or falsity of these statements, his services have not been dispensed with.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) is perfectly right when he says that I am responsible and I accept the sole responsibility for the appointment of Mr. J. B. Jackson. I have not the slightest desire to shelter myself under any diversion of that responsibility. I may add, that, knowing Mr. Jackson very well. I know him to be a very intelligent, capable man, I know that he has filled his office well and will, I think continue to discharge his duties well. As to some of the points to which the hon. gentleman referred I have one or two things to say, There is no doubt whatever that the circumstances connected with the election of Mr. REVISED EDITION

Sutherland, to the local assembly for South Oxford were such as to naturally excite a very considerable amount of suspicion in the minds of those who are acquainted with the history and the details of that country. South Oxford is and has been for a great many years a persistently Liberal county. Mr. McKay, the local member who was defeated, had been returned at the last election by a majority of some 400 or 500-I forget which at the moment. I myself had been but a short time before returned for these portions of tne constituency which were afterwards carried for Mr Sutherland by a very large majority also. Very unexpectedly, very suddenly, we discovered the large majorities for the Liberal candidate were turned into a minority. There was no doubt whatever that large funds had been put up, not by Mr. Sutherland, but by the supporters and friends of Mr. Sutherland, for the purpose of defeating the Ross government, and there was perfect justification for the suspicion that very improper means had been used to elect Mr. Sutherland. Mr. Jackson who was very well acquainted with the constituency, knew who were likely to be concerned in this ; he had been making inquiries and had come on a number of clues that pointed to the fact that a certain gentleman by the name of Chambers knew all about the matter. I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) said that Mr. Chambers was perfectly unknown to Mr. Jackson.

Mr. Chambers lived at Woodstock and Jackson came in and served him with a subpoena and invited him across the street to an hotel and up to that time
they were perfectly unacquainted.
It is the trial report in the ' Globe.'
The trial report in a newspaper is not the judge's charge by any manner of means.
Why is it not the judge's statement ?

The judge's statement it may be, but it is not the judge's statement corroborated by the judge himself. My hon. friend knows very well that these newspaper reports are not to be taken as absolutely reliable on all occasions. I accept what the judge states from the bench as very good evidence of what the judge thought, but I am informed that when the matter came to be reviewed -the trial was conducted before Mr. Justice Britton and Mr. Justice Street-neither of these gentlemen commented on Jackson's proceedings.
Would the hon. gentleman permit me to say that I was present and heard the statement made by Judge Street, and that report is as near as can be, word for word of what he said.
Was that his final charge 7
There is no final charge.
The judge delivers his judgment.
No. I have the statement here from the evidence itself.

If that were the statement corroborated from the shorthand notes taken before the judge, it undoubtedly would be entitled to regard ; but, if it is a simple statement in the newspaper it is not entitled to equal regard no matter what that newspaper may be.
It is in the friendly * Globe.'

Well, it does not matter. If Mr. Jackson had committed an offence punishable by law there were plenty of parties who would have de-
*

sired nothing better than to prosecute Mr. Jackson.
You got him out of the way.

No they bad months and months, and months, and they would have prosecuted him had	he	committed a criminal offence. I made inquiries about the matter and I was informed that whatever indiscretion he may have been guilty of, he had committed no offence contrary to the laws of the land, and I know that these people would have prosecuted Mr. Jackson if he had so done. Nor do I notice that either one or other of the judges stated that Mr. Jackson had left himself open to a prosecution in any shape or way.
You seem to think that Mr. Jackson was a mere martyr.

Mr. Jackson no doubt finding that this constituency had been carried in a very suspicious fashion, and finding that the tracks lay in a particular direction, did go to the party whom he had reason to believe was the most thoroughly acquainted with the whole details, and he did offer him a considerable sum of money it appears for the purpose of obtaining {that evidence ; but Mr. Jackson did not suborn nor did he attempt to suborn testimony.
I quoted from the sworn evidence of the person who said that Jackson asked him not to mention anything about this matter.
All that came before the judges and the judges did not make any such imputation upon Mr. Jackson. Mr. Jackson did attempt to obtain evidence, but he did not attempt to suborn testimony.
Oh.

I would like to know how you are going to obtain evidence in these election trials, unless sometimes men are prepared to pay sums of money for the obtaining of evidence. I venture to say that there are mighty few election trials which are brought to a close in this country in which something of the kind has not to be done. I do not mean to say that it is nice work ; I do not mean to say I like it; I do not mean to say that it is good work, but it is work that has to be done unless you are going to allow these parties on either side to go from one end of the country to another using money for the purpose of illegitimately influencing the electors. You have two choices ; you may prohibit the use of money for obtaining evidence, but if you do, as I said, it practically amounts to granting an amnesty to all parties concerned, to go and bribe just as they please. In this matter Mr. Jackson offered 248J
a sum of money to a party whom he thought could obtain evidence which would unseat Mr. Sutherland. How, and in what way I would like to ask, is Mr. Jackson, morally speaking, more censurable or more culpable than the gentlemen who-unless my memory fails me-offered rewards of several thousand dollars to all parties who would obtain evidence against Liberal candidates at this very same general election ? I think a public advertisement was used ; I think large sums of money were offered ; I think every possible inducement was given to get up cases against the Liberal members. I never heard hon. gentlemen opposite object to that. I never heard these hon. gentlemen dissent from that being an illegitimate means of employing their money, and I cannot for the life of me see in what respect, morally speaking,	Mr. Jackson's conduct was worse than the conduct of those very respected and honourable gentlemen who publicly advertised that they were prepared to pay large sums of money to obtain such evidence as would unseat Liberal members.
Such rascals did not get government appointments.
No ; my hon. friend knows something about government appointments in past times, as the records of the House will show, unless I forget.

You need not forget. I am here and if you want to make that charge, come up into my riding and make it. You are looking for a constituency now, and you can come up to my riding and tell all you know about it, and that won't take you long.
It is on record, and my hon. friend need not distress himself. The matter has been discussed in this House.
The riding has spoken several times, and if you are not in accord with the verdict, come up and try it yourself.	,

My hon. friend must find the cap to fit very tightly, or he would not be so irate at being reminded of what he did in reference to government appointments. It is not the first time, and I suppose it will not be the last on which we shall hear from hon. gentlemen in reference to this matter. No doubt, as I have said, the means that are adopted for obtaining evidence in these; election trials are of a character which I suppose no man on either side of the House wishes to see employed. At the same time, I must point out that the judges stated that in their opinion Mr. Jackson, whatever he had done, had not brought himself within the precincts of the law. nor did the parties who,

were disposed, if they had a fair chance, to prosecute Mr. Jackson, attempt to take any proceedings against him. Unless I am entirely misinformed, these same parties did not put Mr. Chambers into the witness box at all.
Why ?

The
evidence, such as it was, was obtained by Mr. Jackson himself. Why did they not put him into the box ? If I might suggest, they abstained wisely from doing so because in all probability he knew too much. However, be that as it imay, I desire to be clearly understood. 1 exonerate my colleagues entirely in this matter and take the full responsibility of Mr. Jackson's appointment. I say he is a capable man, and if he continues in his office, I think he will justify his appointment. Already I have received on more than one occasion testimony to the ability and diligence with which he is conducting his work. The hon. gentleman did not conclude with a motion ; but I have given him all the information in my power. Such of his facts as were correct I have admitted ; and I have called the attention of the House to the fact that if Mr. Jackson did wrong, his assailants might avail themselves of the courts, but they did not choose to do so, which is the best proof that they knew that whatever faults Mr. Jackson committed, he did not bring himself within the purview of the law.

I received the following from the evidence :
Q. Do I understand you to say that Jackson told you not to say anything about the declaration if you were asked ?-A. If anybody asked me, he told me not to say anything about it.
If he was asked at the inquiry if he had made such a declaration, he was to answer that he had not. There is the evidence of half a dozen other witnesses that Jackson interviewed, and each one of them, when asked that question, presumably at the trial, was to answer that he had not made any declaration. I congratulate the hon. gentleman on his view of political morality in this country.

I was rather amused to notice that when the right hon. gentleman rose in his place he received the applause of his friends ; but I was very much pleased to notice that when he took his seat, his friends did not see fit to applaud him for the stand he had taken.
The professionals applauded him.
They hope to get their jobs.

The hon. member for South Oxford says that Mr. Jackson is a very capable and intelligent man. I quite agree with that. Some years ago my right Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT.
hon. friend had some difficulty in securing the nomination in South Oxford, and be appealed to this capable and intelligent man to manipulate the convention as against his friend Mr. Janes, from the city of Toronto. Mr. Jackson was successful. I do not know whether he encouraged all the criminals that he could get in South Oxford to assist him in securing that convention ; but I do know that he was successful in securing it for the right hon. gentleman, and he is well able to carry out successfully anything he undertakes in the political line. The hon. member for South Oxford says that the constituency is a very safe one. I would ask the right hon. gentleman, from his own experience in politics, whether he would advise his friends to expend large sums of money in a constituency which he claims to have been carried sometimes by hundreds, some times by thousands, and sometimes by acclamation. The right hon. gentleman would not advise his friends to do anything of the kind. That kind of thing is not done on either side. But what occurred in this case ? The representative. Dr. McKay, had paid very little attention to his constituents. In a measure he had ignored them. There was a rumour circulated to the effect that he only required to run his election in order to obtain a government position. Many of his supporters, who had been loyal to him up to that time, disliked that kind of conduct and when Mr. Sutherland, who is a farmer-it is largely a farming constituency-went round the constituency, large numbers of the electors agreed to support him instead of Dr. McKay. These were sufficient to roll up a majority of a hundred or more for Mr. Sutherland. Now, nobody has ever charged Mr. Sutherland with corruption in that election. The proof is in this fact that the trial started on the 15th of October and continued to the 18th, when it was adjourned to December 1st, 2nd and 3rd, after which the argument was adjourned to the city of Toronto. Will any hon. gentleman in this House say, after a careful search made by men like Mr. Jackson, who was connected with the firm of Messrs. Kerr, Davidson, Patterson and Grant, after securing all the assistance which they could by hook or crook, from constables and others, all these days of trial in the city of Woodstock, that Mr. Sutherland was guilty of any charge of corruption without having that charge brought before the judges of the court ? It is simply absurd for any hon. gentleman to talk in that way. There was only one charge proved against Mr. Sutherland's friends ; that was, the hiring of a livery in the town of Ingersoll. I think that pretty conclusively proves the statement of my hon. friend if there was anything suspicious in connection with that election in South Oxford, it is not borne out by the evidence which was brought out in the court held in the city of Woodstock. Now, if my hon. friend's statement is correct that

large sums of money were supposed to have been spent in tbe case of Mr. Sutherland to corrupt the vote, this is the only instance. With reference to Mr. Chambers being practically unacquainted with Mr. Jackson, let me say that Mr. Chambers was acquainted with Mr. Jackson and Mr. Jackson was acquainted with Mr. Chambers.
At One o'clock, House took recess.
House resumed at Three o'clock.

When you left the chair at one o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was leading up to the difference between the explanation of the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce and that of the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett), regarding degree of acquaintance between Mr. Chambers and Mr. Jackson. The hon. member tor East Simcoe was quite right in assuming that these gentlemen were not well acquainted with each other. When he read the declaration of Mr. Chambers, he found these words in it :
He then asked me to come with him to the Dufferin Hotel and have a smoke. When we reached there, he asked if there was a private room, and on being shown one we both went m alone. He talked with me very familiarly, call ing me by my first name.
From these words one would naturally conclude that Mr. Jackson had assumed a familiarity with Mr. Chambers which he had not been in the habit of doing, and consequently the hon. gentleman was quite justified in concluding that the two men were strangers. I know from my personal knowledge that they were acquaintances, but I am quite well satisfied that they wei not familiar acquaintances. My right lion, friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce tried to make a point out of the fact h tbe respondents counsel did not place Cham bers in the box on that occasion. But he did not say why Chambers' evidence was not admissible. His evidence was offered in court, he was called, but the fact ot Mr. Jackson not being the respondent case and not being on trial, rendered Chambers' evidence not admissible. In other words, it was collateral evidence and not admissible on that occasion But I can go so far as to say that if the evidence of Messrs. Chambers, Francis and Smith had been admitted, they would have proven beyond doubt that Jackson had made the statement that he was prepared to pay for any evidence wliicb would unseat Mi. Sutherland, whether that evidence was true or false. I was amazed when my right hon. friend, in his jocular way, condoned the conduct of Mr. Jackson. I was amazed to hear him condone the obtaining of evidence in that way. I was grieved to hear the right hon. gentleman (Sir Richard Cartwright) view it in that light, and I must confess I had a better opinion of
my right hon. friend. It is a well known fact that judges do not approve of statements being taken down by lawyers on behalf of witnesses. It is well known that they do not approve of lawyers taking affidavits or declarations. They prefer that the witnesses should be placed in the box and give evidence themseives and be free to state what they believe to be the truth; but my right hon. friend (Sir Richard Cartwright) seems to approve of the solicitor for the petitioners in this case obtaining affidavits from men-who are telling the truth. Now, the sole object was to obtain affidavits from men who, Mr. Jackson knew, were not to tell the truth, and he was .paying them to make such affidavits and to be prepared to stick to them, should they be called into court as witnesses. - , There is another case, that of Mr. King. The hon member from East Simcoe mentioned Mr. King. Mr. King is a highly respected citizen of Ingersoll. He )s a merchant and a gentleman whom the citizens honoured by electing him as mayor, and he represented that town as mayor foi some time. Well, what do we find Mr. Jackson doing ? We find him going to a man of the name of Collins, whose criminal offences have been quoted in this House, and inducing that man to make a statement against one of the most respected citizens of Ingersoll. And who did Jackson get to corroborate this statement of Collins ? No other than Collins's wife, who was also a criminal, as was shown in court. And we have these two criminals giving evidence against one of the most honoured and respected citizens of the town-one whom the people of Ingersoll, largely Liberal, elected as their mayor, although he is a Conservative thus showing their confidence in his honesty and ability. Yet in order to unseat Mr. Sutherland, these two criminals were brought in to swear falsely against a respected citizen of the town of Ingersoll. Why was all this done ? Because the Ontario government was only sustained in the general elections by two of a majority, and owing to the death of Mr. Munroe. of Renfrew, that majority was reduced to one. In order to save themselves they attacked Mr. Sutherland in the county of Oxford. They attacked him in order to unseat him, because, as my right hon. friend has said, South Oxford has a Liberal majority, and they thought, if they could unseat Mr. Sutherland by any means, good or bad, they would be, in a position to elect in his place a supporter of the Ontario government. That is what the Ontario government had at stake. And what had Mr. Jackson at stake ? He had a judgeship at stake. He was working for his reward from this government. There, is no use trying to deny the facts. We have in this House a gentleman, occupying one of the highest positions in the government of Can-

ada, honoured by the imperial authorities with a title (Sir Richard Cartwright), coming forward and admitting that he knew all the facts in connection with the case and took full responsibility. Was this the reason why this government rewarded this gentleman ? I do not believe that it was the sole reason. I am inclined to believe that services rendered, untold events which occurred in some years gone by-and which Mr. Jackson threatened to expose, if not rewarded-had something to do with his appointment. Mr. Jackson knew that he could not secure a judgeship. He knew that the Ontario government dared not with its small majority of one, appoint him to any position under it. He therefore came to Ottawa, and inside of a year was appointed to an important position in England. What was that important position ? I find this inquiry put by the Hon. Sir Mackenzie Bowell in the Senate :
Whether a man by the name of J. B. Jackson, of Ingersoll, Ontario, has been appointed to any position in England or elsewhere, by the government of Canada, or any member of said government ?
If so, what are the duties assigned to him, and what salary or remuneration is he to receive for the performance of such services ?
Hon. Mr. SCOTT-J. B. Jackson, of Jngersoll, Ontario, was appointed by Order in Council of date October 31st, 1903 (appointment to date from 1st November, 1903) commercial agent to Leeds and Hull, England.
His duties are to report monthly, or more frequently, if necessary, to the Department of Trade and Commerce upon ail trade matters which may be of interest to Canadian exporters, and to use his best endeavour to further Canada's market in the district to which he is assigned. These reports are published weekly and are sent to any business men in Canada desiring them.
Mr. Jackson's salary is $3,000 per annum, and office and contingent expenses. I
I have made hard statements about this man. I call upon my witnesses to substantiate the statement I am making and if the right hon. gentleman will communicate with Mr. Ball, county Crown attorney for Oxford, I believe that he will get some information about Mr. J. B. Jackson. He will find that Mr. J. B. Jackson was charged with forgery or perjury and that owing to the theft of a certain document during the night Jackson escaped being committed for the crime with which he was charged. If my right hon. friend will communicate with Mr. Ball, Mr. Ball will tell him that Jackson is a scoundrel. And yet, Sir, this gentleman whom I find in the 'Parliamentary Companion ' to bear this title :
Rt. Hon. Sir Richard John Cartwright, G.C.M., P.C.
Privy Councillor, who has received one of the highest titles in the gift of the imperial authorities as bestowed on Canadian subjects, a gentleman who has filled the im-Mr. INGRAM.
portant position of Finance Minister of Canada, and who to-day is filling a responsible position of Minister of Trade and Commerce, has appointed this man Jackson to an important position. I ask my hon. friends who have heard the evidence that has been shown in this House to-day, after witnessing the flippant manner in which that right hon. gentleman spoke in connection with the appointment of this man Jackson, do they think it will be a very nice thing for the imperial authorities, who have bestowed this title on the right hon. gentleman, to read the evidence in connection with J. B. Jackson ? Do hon. gentlemen think that the imperial authorities will consider that the title has been well bestowed upon a man who by his own assertion to-day has condoned the purchasing of perjury and offences of this kind ? Reference has been made to the confusion of Ontario and Dominion politics and the Conservatives in this House have been blamed for dragging in the provincial government in matters of this kind. I remember in days gone by when the Liberal party in this House condemned the Dominion and local authorities for travelling in couples. I remember those days quite well, but, Sir, who were the first to drag into the same arena local and Dominion issues and make them as one ? The very party of which the right hon. gentleman is one of the chief leaders. Who are they selecting as candidates for this country ? I go to London and find that the governor of the county jail in Middlesex is the Dominion candidate in North Middlesex. I go to the constituency of my hon. friend from Halton and find opposing him the public school inspector receiving pay from the Ontario government. I go to Dundas, and find as the Liberal candidate the provincial inspector of jails and asylums, Dr. Chamberlain. These men drawing money for their services from the local government are now candidates for this House on behalf of the Liberal party. And yet hon. gentlemen talk to us about associating local and Dominion politics !
There is another important question. As I said the hon. gentlemen opposite applauded the right hon. gentleman when he rose to reply to the remarks of the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett), but I wish to congratulate hon. gentle'men behind him upon the fact that they did not applaud the right hon. gentleman after he made Bis explanation in this House, and I am sure when the statement made by him is quoted against him in this country-and it will be because it deserves to be-showing the depth to which these hon. gentlemen have descended, and showing the disregard they have for what is proper and right and the degradation that will attach to any man who is a member of a party whose leaders express such sentiments. This chamber has rung day after day during this session because we have found that a government
, JULY 28, 1904
employee of this country had the audacity to write a letter or to find fault in connection with certain political interference with his duties connected with his office. We were told by the Liberal press that these officials had disgraced themselves. The people of this city were only the other day warned not to join in a procession in honour of a man who had disgraced Canada by finding fault with the political influences used in his department. Every word of that paper was in condemnation of those who turned out to give a send-off to that man because he had disgraced himself. I have yet to learn that Lord Dundonald has arrived at the stage of having bought perjured evidence in this country to unseat a good man. What he has done has been an honourable thing.
