He is condemned for that and yet we find praise and reward for the man who had purchased perjured evidence. Now, Sir, I do not wish to pursue this matter any further. The right hon. gentleman has relieved us from believing that he was not aware of what occurred on that memorable occasion and I have only to say to him that the electors of South Oxford will not compliment him for saying that money was put into that constituency for the purpose of purchasing the honest electors of South Oxford.

There was a time in the history of Canada when the Reform party were credited with standing for honour and honesty if for nothing else. The 'people of the country believed that the more prominent men of the party were men of sterling honour and sterling integrity and certainly in the public life of Canada so far as Canada knew they were examples of honesty, examples that might well be copied by the rising generations. But unfortunately of late years they seem to have drifted away from their moorings, and those who were the leading lights in the party in the past appear to vie with each other today in their degradation and their lowering of the public life of Canada, in discrediting the honour of Canadian public men and disgracing party politics. That is the position as it appears to-day. What is the qualification for appointment to office to-day ? Appointments to office are made strictly I believe for party purposes, and I am speaking advisedly when I say so. If I were requested to give an example I might name them by the dozen and the greater the scoundrel, the more successful he has been in wrongdoing for his political party, the more successful he has been in accomplishing in an improper way what they desire to have accomplished, the success of the party, the greater seems to be his qualification for a position of trust and o,f honour. Need I give examples of it ? Take, for instance, the one that we have been discussing this afternoon. Take Mr. Preston, if you like) who occupies a very prominent position as an immigration agent of Canada to-day.
For years and years, to the disgrace of the party and the disgrace of Mr. Preston, he was one of the most unscrupulous men, L believe, not only in the province of Ontario, but in the Dominion of Canada, a man whose word was of no account, whose honour seemed to be so light that no person respected it, a man whose own uncle went into court and produced not less than ten or twelve respectable witnesses who made affidavits to the effect that they would: not believe him on his oath. That Is the reputation of the man who has been honoured by being appointed to a prominent position and to-day he is pensioned on the country at a salary of 83,000 a year and office and other expenses, as an immigration agent in England.
And he is one of the best we ever had.
One of the best we ever-had according to the judgment of the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell). And when the country knows that, I need say no more.
They do know it.

I say that that man who came back here and entered a suit against a party in this city to vindicate his character

 i

His what ?
Mr. SPROULE

and he dared not go
on with the suit for fear that his character which he wished to vindicate would only be shown to be blacker than it was considered to be up to that time.
If Mr. Preston was here you would not dare to say that to him outside the chamber.
I have said the same thing to Mr. Preston face to face. I do not need to hide behind the privileges of parliament. Mr. Preston knows it too well, and the hon. member knows it too.
You are very bold in the House of Commons, but you would not be so bold outside.

I may be told that had the suit been tried Mr. Preston would: have been cleared. What are the facts ?' The record stands to-day in the courts of this country that twelve presumably honest men went into the court and swore they would not believe him on his oath, his own uncle and other witnesses to the number of ten or twelve. This is fihe man who did the dirty work for the party for years, and travelled in filth and mire up to his neck ; and this is the man who to-day is honoured by holding the high position of representative of Canada In England, and who is writing letters to discredit 1 a man like Lord Dundonald. This is the

civil servant who did the dirty work of the party and whom they celebrated to-day, he believing that he will be shielded by his party as he has been in the past. That is an example of what is going on in our decaying and decadent public and political life in Canada as a consequence of the party who are in power to-day.
Then we take Jackson whose case is before the House for consideration at the present time, and we hear an hon. knight dedaring : I assume full responsibility for Jackson's appointment, and I defend it. And what does he add ? He is an intelligent and capable man ? On hearing that I said mentally : It is a great pity he could not say that he is an honest and truthful man. Could he do it ? No, he dare not risk his reputation by saying that, because there is too much on record to prove the contrary -a man who stands disgraced before the public of Canada to-day, a man who has not only perjured himself but endeavoured to purchase others to commit perjury as well, a man who is a forger himself, and had the documents not been improperly stolen or taken away from the public office, documents that are in the custody of friends of the hon. gentleman, that would have been proven in court, and I presume Jackson would have been in the penitentiary to-day instead of receiving the salary that he does over in England. And this is the man of whom the knight says : I assume the full responsibility of his appointment, I am prepared to assume it. Then if we go back in history a little, what do we find ? We are told this is the man who succeeded by his peculiar methods in political life, Or who helped others to succeed in getting the knight elected in South Oxford, for the last time -the Wandering Willie of his party, who, like Noah's dove, found no rest for the sole of his foot until he found it in South Oxford by virtue of the machinations of such men as Jackson, who to-day is reaping his reward. No wonder the hon. gentleman assumes responsibility for his appointment. There is a debt of gratitude due to Jackson from the hon. gentleman that he dare not withhold. Jackson knows too much to be left in the cold and friendless world, he must be taken care of, and he is taken care of, and the hon. member to-day assumes the full responsibility of his appointment. I can tell him that, talking a short time ago with some of the honest Reformers in South Oxford, they declared publicly to me that it was one of the most disgraceful appointments ever made in Canada, and on no man does that disgrace rest with greater weight than upon the hon. member for South Oxford.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The Prime Minister is responsible.

Yes, and every other member of that cabinet, and they must be Mr. SPROULE.
held responsible for it to the public of Canada, because that is what they have brought upon Canada by such appointments. Then we take others of the same ilk, because they are hunting in couples to-day, they are employing the same degraded characters to do the dirty work for the party in the Dominion as well as the provinces. Take Pritchett, take Tom Lewis, take the notorious Grant, who has always been the handy man of the party, ready to do their dirty work, take Captain Sullivan, take Frank Sullivan, take the whole gang of them, and what are they ? Every one of them, the deeper they are steeped in political crime in the service of their political party the more eligible they are for high appointments in the gift of the party.
Masters of the administration.

Mr. Speaker, the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) has accepted the full responsibility for the appointment of this gentleman to the lucrative position which he now holds. It may be advisable for us to review that appointment very briefly in the light of what was disclosed at the trial which has already been referred to. Mr. Jackson, who was a solicitor, had charge of the petition, and his chief assistants in the local preparation of the case were a constable named Ellis Fick, of Tilsonburg, another man named Charles Hewlett, a prominent Liberal worker in the Tiding, and a professional machine man, as he is called, in the riding, named George Sutherland. The trial opened at Woodstock on the 15th October and continued for several days. The evidence and declarations which I have in my hand disclose the following facts in regard to Mr. Jackson :
He personally paid money to George Fournier, a criminal character, one of his witnesses in the protest. A man by the name of Parker, another named Elijah Harp, and others, swore that Fournier offered them money to swear to falsehoods. I have the evidence for that under my hand, and I have the pages to refer to if any hon. gentleman sees fit to deny or discredit that statement. Jackson paid Charles Parker $10, or, according to his own admission, $5 for similar purposes. I have the'evidence to give in answer to any person who will undertake to contradict that statement. He paid Ellis Fick, by his own admission, $250, and according to the evidence of Charles Parker and William Abraham Young and others, Fick endeavoured to bribe them to swear to falsehoods. The right hon. gentleman has referred to witnesses not being put in the box. Let me remind him that when this evidence was given in this case the petitioner did not put Fick in the box to contradict this statement, but, on the contrary, Fick was found con- [DOT] veniently absent as soon as this evidence had been given. Mr. Jackson had Charles Hewlett and George Sutherland assisting

him in preparing the protest, and he himself interviewed witnesses, F. R. Avey and Lincoln Pollard, who admitted on oath that Hewlett had paid them money to make declarations. A large number of witnesses, among them Parker, Young, Avey, Pollard and Mustard, admitted on oath that Hewlett and Sutherland had bribed and attempted to bribe them to give evidence, and their statements were not attempted to be denied. In fact, the evidence shows that Hewlett and Sutherland absented or concealed themselves, so that the respondent could not subpoena them for the adjourned trial. It should also be remembered that Sutherland did a great deal of his work in the office of Mr. Jackson himself.
Mr. Jackson himself paid Edward Chambers $8 i.>
cash, and promised him $375 more on condition that Chambers should get evidence which would prove eight charges. This agreement with Chambers was to be private : in fact, there was a written declaration drawn up that nothing was to be said about it. Mr. Jackson admits that the last $375 was to be paid only on condition that Chambers would prove eight certain charges. Jackson told Chambers that it did not matter whether the evidence was true or false so long as it answered the purpose. Mr. Chambers is corroborated on oath as to this by two other reputable gentlemen of Woodstock, Mr. Vaughn Francis and Mr. Samuel Smith, who declare that they overheard Jackson distinctly tell Chambers that it did not matter whether the evidence were false or true, so long as it unseated Sutherland. The right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce is, now willing to accept responsibility for' that. I should say, in justice to Mr. Jackson, that he denied this statement, but he was met with the distinct statement to the contrary of no less than three witnesses. He disbursed an enormous amount of money in connection with the campaign, and he states that he kept no record of his disbursements. He interviewed Frederick R. Avey, a bribed witness, at Avey's house, and, as Avey swears, told Avey he was not to say that he had been given anything for giving his evidence. He interviewed Lincoln Pollard, another bribed witness, and, according to Pollard, told Pollard if any one asked him about it to say nothing about making the declaration. I would be inclined to think that the right hon. gentleman is accepting a pretty fair share of responsibility when he undertakes to shoulder all that.
Let me call his attention to some of the sworn evidence, to which I will just briefly refer in order that this evidence may impress itself a little more upon him. Edward William Chambers made a sworn declaration on the Uth October, 1902, from which I shall read. On Friday evening, before thp trial opened, and the trial opened on the 15th October, he had an interview with Mr. Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
Jackson. He told Mr. Vaughn Francis of the proposed interview, and he arranged to have Mr. Francis and Mr. Samuel Smith come to his house on that Friday evening, in order that they might hear what Mr. Jackson had to offer. He goes on to say that they were in a position to hear what took place, and he details in his affidavit the conversation as follows :
After a general conversation Jackson wanted me to sign an agreement not to divulge the conversation, which I refused to do, and then Jackson wanted to know how much I wanted to get him evidence to unseat Sutherland. I told him $5,000. He said that was out of the question. He then said that he thought $500 down, and $1,500 additional if the evidence was sufficient to unseat Suth-land.
That is paragraph 4 of the declaration and paragraph 5 is as follows :
I 'then asked him what class of evidence he wanted, whether false or true, and he said it mattered not to him whether it was false or true so long as he could unseat Sutherland. He said he would lose his gown if this conversation was divulged.
Let me point out to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, that by the sworn declaration of Mr. Vaughn L. Francis under date of 11th October, 1902, that statement is expressly and absolutely confirmed, and by the sworn statement of Mr. Samuel Wm. Smith under date 11th of October, 1902, that statement is also confirmed. I shall refer to one or two passages in the evidence taken in the trial. I quote from the evidence of Chas. Parker.
Q. What proposal did he make to you ?
A. Well, he asked me if I received anything for my vote and I told him I did not.
Q. What next did he say to you ?
A. Well, he asked me if I would say that I had.
This was not a proposal made by Mr. Jackson himself but it was a proposal made by one of the men whom he had hired and paid for the purpose of obtaining evidence in this case. In the evidence of Mr. Jackson himself he was asked with reference to his conversation with Mr. Chambers.
Q. Didn't he ask for $5,000 or $10,000 or a larger amount ?
A. $5,000 may have been mentioned, but I am sure that $1,500 and $2,000 was mentioned.
Q. How much did you promise to give him ?
A. I gave him $375 and, I promised to give him $375 more if he could produce evidence to substantiate the eight charges he gave me.
Further on :
Q. You paid him $375 down and you were to pay him the balance on what condition ?
A. On condition that the eight charges should be proved.
Let me point out to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that he himself has stated that applications of this kind are made to persons of a certain character; persons

who are not to be too much trusted, and here is this gentleman for whose appointment the minister takes full responsibility, going to one of these men so characterized by the Minister of Trade and Commerce-* although I believe him to be a reputable citizen-Jackson goes to this citizen who is supposed to be influenced, and he pays him $375 down and promises him the same amount in addition if he will produce evidence that will unseat Mr. Sutherland. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has no adjectives to apply to conduct of that kind, except ' indiscreet.' That is all that the English language will furnish the right hon. gentleman for conduct of that character and for an occasion of that kind-his vocabulary is not so bare on other occasions. In the evidence of Mr. Frederick R. Avey, is to be found the following :
Q. Do you know Mr. Jackson, the lawyer of Ingersoll ?
A. Yes.
Q. He stated to you as I am instructed that you were not to say that you had been given anything for swearing for them ?
A. He did.
Q. When was that ?
A. Well, it was a week ago last Tuesday night, or two weeks.
Q. Where did he give you these instructions?
A. At my house .
. Further on :
Q. Did he speak to you about the declaration which you had given to Mr. Hewlett ?
Mr. Hewlett was one of the paid agents of Mr. Jackson.
A. Yes.
Q- What did he say about that ? He knew all about it then ?
A. Yes.
Q. What did he say about it ?
A. He said : If they ask did you make a declaration, you need not tell them ; somthing like that.
Further on :
Well, he says, if they'ask you whether you got anything for it or not, tell them that you did not.
Further on another witness whose name I do not recollect was examined by Mr. Watson counsel for petitioner.
Q. There is just one question ; in the meantime do I understand you to say that Mr. Jackson told you not to say anything about the declaration if you were asked ?
A. If anybody asked me he told me not to say anything about it.
And so on, and all through this evidence one could quote ad libitum statements of precisely a similar character. It seems to me that the position which the Minister of Trade and Commerce has taken with regard to this matter is of an extraordinary nature. In fact he has invented a new decalogue ; so far as the commandments forbid, he would abolish them all
and insert instead : ' Thou shalt be discreet so that thou shalt not be found out.' The Minister of Trade and Commerce has no word of criticism upon Mr. Jackson for asking these men to procure evidence, whether true or false, so long as it should unseat Mr. Sutherland. He has no word of criticism with regard to that, but he has a reproach against Jackson because he did not look up the chimney, because he did not look in the cellar to see if any one was listening ; in short, because he was indiscreet. In other words if we are to take the right hon. gentleman at his own valuation he is perfectly content that Mr. Jackson should purchase evidence that he should incite these men to procure evidence whether true or false ; and the only requirement necessary for promotion in the civil service of Canada is that it shall be done so that it cannot be proven. Well, the right hon. gentleman is eloquent sometimes ; he is severe sometimes ; I think he told us since last session that on this side of the House we were a lot of nobodies, heard of nowhere outside of our own parishes. I say to the right hon. gentleman the Minister of Trade and Commerce, that it had been better for him as a public man in this country if he had retired to the isolation of his own parish and been heard of no more, before he made the declaration which he has to-day made in this House. I believe, Sir, that there never was in the public life of this country or of any other country a more damnable doctrine more unblushingly avowed. I do not understand how a gentleman who has had his experience in public life, who has in the past preached lofty doctrines with regard to purity of public life and in the administration of public affairs, could ever have found it in his heart to stand up in this House of Commons, and to make the avowal which the Minister of Trade and Commerce has made to-day. It was bold ; it was more than bold, it was unblushing, and if I were not transgressing parliamentary decorum I would say that it was utterly shameless. That this man, so stigmatized by Mr. Justice Street, should be promoted to the public service of Canada, and that the Minister of Trade and Commerce speaking for the government should not be ashamed to stand up and justify him, is an unheard of degradation in our public life. We are indebted to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) for bringing the matter to the attention of the House, and in my opinion, it deserves grave consideration from the House and the country. To testify my appreciation of the importance of the question, I beg to move :
That all the words in the resolution after the word ' that ' be omitted and the following substituted therefor : -
That in making appointments to pubic offices, and particularly to those of a representative nature, party services should not alone he considered, but selections should be made

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know anything about the population there now, but

It seems to me that in regard to this work involving a very large expenditure one would have expected to have received better advice from the engineering staff. They should have made 240-

man will understand that there is a difference between an expenditure on a harbour in the way of dredging, although it may not be a government-owned harbour, and an expenditure on a wharf which is not owned by the government. Ontario-Sarnia, dredging, $12,000.
This is being done by contract.

The channel entering the canal. This is for dredging from the head of the wharf to the channel. The actual work in the channel comes under the Department of Railways and Canals. This is for the extension of the wharf and dredging twenty feet from the wharf to the channel.

This will not complete the wliarf. One of the objects of extending the wharf was to lessen the amount of dredging. This amount will cover all that can be expended during the present year, and a further amount of about $39,000 will be required to complete.

Two hundred and fifty feet,

By the yard ?

As Saugeen river improvements. We thought it better to take a vote for Saugeen river so that there would be no misunderstanding.

This is the fourth session that this item has appeared in the estimates. It seems to be held there as bait or something of that kind without any intention of spending the money. Three years ago we were told that this money would be spent at once.
Well, we are perfectly frank about it, and I am moving to strike it out on the report of the engineers.

Motion agreed to, and item struck out.

The difficulty here is that we have not so far been able to find a dredge available to do the work.
Have yon any assurance of being able to get a dredge this coming summer ?
It is almost impossible to get dredges to take small contracts of this kind, owing to the cost of towing, loss of time, &c., in going from place to place.

I can appreciate the difficulty of getting dredges, because I know there is a dearth of them in that district, but at the same time, I object- to the principle of taking money from year to year, unless the government- are satisfied they can go on with the work because otherwise it becomes a temptation and is used in favour of the government at election times.
I have often heard the hon. member for South Oxford (Sir Richard Cartwright) in the strongest language denounce this practice, and I think he was justified in doing it.
I agreed with him and still entertain that opinion. We have these items by the dozen, money voted year after year and not spent. When they ask for money they should make an effort to spend it, and they should not ask for it unless they are in a position to go on with the work.

The hon. gentleman is perfectly right in saying there are certain amounts in the estimates, but the great difficulty is with such a large number of works to get them all going. It takes a considerable amount of time in the department to prepare the plans, but the engineers lose no time in their work. But, of course there must be delay in a case of this kind where a dredge is not available.

$5,000 the whole vote.

I aln informed the work is completed.

Last session the member representing that riding objected to this vote, I am not sure he moved to strike it out but he opposed the item and the Minister of Public Works promised this committee that no more money would be spent on this until he went up himself personally and investigated it. Could the acting minister inform the committee whether that promise has been carried out or not, whether the minister has himself gone up and investigated it ?

The department has simply employed sufficient labour to use the materials that were on the ground. It was felt that it would not be right after making an expenditure of that amount to let the material go to waste.

We were well aware of that last year. But the matter has been brought before the committee last year, that the promoter of that work was not very reliable and that he had in some way misled this government. The Minister of Works agreed with this committee that under these circumstances, having been informed that the promoter was not reliable, and had made statements that were not at all likely to be correct, he himself would

go up before the material was made use or* and investigate. I shall read the minister's words with reference to the promoter last year. He said, referring to Mr. Can-tin :

This man is no doubt a good deal of the character the hon. gentleman (Mr. McEwen) spoke of. He seems to be able to live by his wits and to induct people to put money in schemes that have little foundation. I do not know him myself or anything about him except what I hav-* heard in connection with this matter. He deceived a great many people into putting money into this scheme. It is stated now that a good many substantial people have taken hold of the work, and I think we might probably take a vote and spend it on the conditions as to whether they are going on to develop this place and the work will help to do so. Now that we have spent so much money wc might go on.
Tliis Is the opinion given by the Minister of Public Works and after some further remarks by Mr. McEwen in opposition to the vote, the minister says :

There has been ov,er $10,000 expended on the work, but I am perfectly willing, if the item passes, to have an inquiry into all the circumstances, and if this work is not in the public interest, I will not finish it. The chief engineer of the department says that there are ten or eleven feet of water there, and I cannot understand how he could have made such a report if there is none.
Mr. McEwen said on that occasion :
As far as I am personally concerned, if the hon. minister will go up there and see for himself, I am willing to let the item drop.
That is the hon. member's statement. Now we will see' what the hon. minister says further :

I am perfectly willing to go up there and consult the hon. members of the riding before anything further is done.
In another place he says, in answer to Mr. McEwen :
If the hon. gentleman thinks that I should go instead of the chief engineer, I am quite willing to do so.
Now, there was a straight promise to go up there and investigate. He knew the circumstances very well, there has been nothing revealed since. All the material was lying there at the time, there has been no other material furnished since that discussion took place. The minister promised that he woqld go there before he spent a dollar of money. Under these circumstances we allowed the matter to pass, being satisfied that if he went up there and investigated for himself he would not spend a dollar of money. Now, it is unnecessary for me to say that the people up there look with a good deal of disfavour upon the government spending public money there. If the people in that part of the country asked for that Mr. SHERRITT.
amount of money, do you think the member representing that riding would get up here on the floor of the House and ofipose it, as he did oppose it in every possible way ? Do you think that I would risk my reputation amongst the people there by opposing it, as I live only a short distance away from the work ? The thing is very unpopular there. It is an extraordinary state of affairs that, notwithstanding a promise made in the House by the Minister of Public Works, this work should go on and money should be spent there. To my mind it is ail awful state of affairs if we cannot believe a minister's statement.
Oh, I think that is rather hard.
I will take that back- if we cannot rely upon the promise of the minister to go up there and see for himself.

Under ordinary circumstances possibly the hon. gentleman might be justified in making these rather harsh comments. But I would like him to remember that the Minister of Public Works has not been in good health for some time. The hon. gentleman knows that for the last two or three months he has been entirely unable to give serious attention to his department, and under these circumstances i think the hon. gentleman might have been a little milder in his criticism. When the minister gave that promise I am quite sure he intended to carry it out and to go there and see this work. Unfortunately for the last three or four weeks he has been obliged to be away a good deal of the time.
I do not remember myself authorizing the work, but I remember the condition of affairs was brought to my attention, and I was told that this amount of material was lying there, and that the engineer had reported that it was in the interest of the country that the work should be proceeded with instead of allowing the material to go to waste. I know there has been considerable criticism of this vote, but it must be remembered that at that time a large amount of money had been spent and a considerable amount of material was on the ground.

I have no doubt that the minister at the time intended to carry out ,his promise made in the House. But it seems to me if he could not go himself he might have sent some one. When he stated in the House that he would not spend any more money without discussing the matter with the member for the riding-of course I do not represent the riding-I thought that he might at least have given us some idea of his intention. I assure you again, Mr. Chairman, that the people in that locality look upon this expenditure as a throw-away of money. May I ask the

minister what is the condition of the harbour there now, what depth of water is there now ?
I am informed there is from ten to eleven feet at the outer end of the pier.

The year before last the same question was discussed In this House at length, and the then Minister of Public Works told us most positively that he would have a report made upon that harbour, and if the circumstances were found to be as alleged no money would be spent. Still he went on and spent the money. When we came back to this House that minister is out and another takes his place.
The minister is not out, he is ill.

I am correct, I say the minister who gave this promise to the House was out and another was in his place when we came back again. Now we have the same discussion over again. More money was asked for and the money which was voted the year before last was spent, notwithstanding the promise that had been made. Another sum was voted last year, and we had a similar promise made by this minister, and we come back this year to find that the money is spent again, and that the minister has not carried out his word. So we are being jollied along from year to year, promises are made which are not kept, and in the meantime the money is being squandered.
When was this money expended, the $5,000 that has been expended since the last session of parliament ?
In the months of April, May and June of this year.

Well, I think this is a very strange manner of conducting public business. In addition to what my hon. friend from North Middlesex (Mr. Sherritt) has read, I want to read a statement from the member for South Huron (Mr. McEwen). Last year, speaking about the promise that was given to the government when they first proposed to construct this work, the hon. gentleman said :
They have not yet established a manufactory of any kind or any other thing that would require a wharf.
Further on he says :
As to the wharf, there has been $10,000 spent, and I am very sorry to say that the money has been unwisely spent. I could not approve of this expenditure, because nine out of ten of my constituents believe that the money has been unwdsely expended.
Now, here is a statement from the hon. gentleman vdio represents the county and is a supporter of the minister himself. Leaving out the fact that this gentleman
was sufficiently influential with the government to get the work commenced, I will just read what the member for South Huron says about the matter :
What surprises me is that a man of his kind'should be able to mislead this government into spending money where there is no need for it at the present time or for years to come.
It is a little unfortunate that the minister and his supporters should expend money in so many places where it is not required, even according to the statements of the hon. gentleman who represents the county, and leave other places unprovided for where the money is required in the public interest. According to the testimony of the hon. gentleman on that side of the House who represents the county, it appears that the government were misled by this gentleman into an expenditure of $10,000. The hon. gentleman stood up in his place at the last session and condemned the government for undertaking this work, and as my hon. friend from East Grey has pointed out, we had a promise from the hon. Minister of Public Works two years ago, and another promise last year that no further money would be expended until an examination of the work had taken place, but in the face of the statement of the hon. gentleman representing the county that the wharf is of no value, that it is not required now, that it will not be required for years to come, and in face of the further statement in reference to the $10,000 that has been expended we are asked to put $5,000 more into the work. The hon. member who represents the county said last year :
As to tbe wharf there has been $1 0,000, spent, and I am very sorry to say that the money has been unwisely spent. There are seven or eight cribs on the shore, and one crib in two or three feet of water, and that is the whole result of the expenditure of $10,000.
In the face of that statement, the hon. gentleman and his supporters will go into that county, and spend $5,000 more of public money, having before them the bald statement of the hon. gentleman representing that county that the wharf is of no value to the people, and knowing that the promises given by the gentleman who induced the-government to spend this $10,000 have not been fulfilled. Then the hon. minister appeals to the electors again by saying : We will consider it further and we will, perhaps,, spend some more money.
I am sure the hon. gentleman does not wish to put words in my mouth that I did not utter.

I do not wish to misrepresent the hon. gentleman, but I thought his remarks suggested something in reference to what might take place in the fall or at some time in the near future. I think this

is a wasteful expenditure of money. There can be no justification for it whatever. In face of the statement made by the hon. gentleman who represents the county on May 19, 1903, the government send a representative up there, and they say to the department: Go on and spend the money. No matter about the $10,000 ; let it go. We have evidence that the wharf is not required, and we have the evidence from the county representative that the wharf is of no value to the residents there. Although this work will be of no use to the public, it will be a monument to an extravagant government which has money to spend in counties where a work is not required and which is neglecting some other counties where money wisely expended would be in the public interest. I hope the hon. minister will learn new lessons of economy since he has taken charge of the department. I hope that next year he will not venture to bring such illustrations of economic government before the people of this country as this one is.
Ontario-Thessalon-breakwater, $15,000.
Under contract.

The building of a pier. The contract amounts to $19,000. The total probable cost will be about $21,000. There was voted in the main estimates $15,000, and in the supplementary estimates there will be $5,500 to complete.
Who has the contract ?

Boyle Brothers, Sault Ste. Marie.
Ontario-Thornbury, dredging, $3,550.
How is that dredging done ?

-It is done by a hired dredge.
Mr. -SPROULE. I notice that you did not do this dredging last year. I suppose that was because you could not get a dredge ?
That was the reason.
This happens to be in my riding, and of course I know the necessities of the case better than those who are not acquainted with the locality.
If the hon. gentleman can suggest where we can get a dredge, I shall be very glad to do the work.
If I could I would be very glad to do so, but I do not know where the dredges are located. I do know the necessities of the people of Thornbury.
I was not here when the Collingwood item was under consideration, but I would like to ask the hon. minister if he can state to the committee what is the valuation of the dry-dock at Collingwood ?
The information was promised to me tonight.

I have not the information, but I will be very glad to bring down a memorandum to-morrow.
Ontario-Toronto harbour-works at eastern entrance, &c., $28,000.

Before this item is adopted, I would like to draw the attention of the hon. minister to a paragraph I see in the Ottawa correspondence of the Toronto ' News,' which bears upon it. It is as follows :
In the main estimates brought down some months ago there is an item of $28,000 for Toronto harbour works at the eastern entrance, and, according to the departmental officials, this item will' cover dredging generally, repairs to the two piers at the eastern gap and repairs to the breakwater from the eastern entrance westward. No further - item appears in the supplementaries. The department is advised by its own engineers and by other engineers who have studied the question, that the ultimate solution of the protection of the island must be found in the construction of a continuous breakwater from end to end of the island. For the present, however, the government does not seem disposed to invite the necessary vote. The present item, which may be reached in discussion to-day, is not thought to he large enough to permit any enlargements of the breakwater. That portion of it which will be applied to the breakwater will be for repairs done.	.
I would like to ask the hon. minister what amount has already been expended for repairs under that' item of $28,000 ?

The expenditure from the 1st of July to the 31st December, 1903, was $13,041, and up to the 30th of June it is estimated that the expenditure will have been $10,900. That will be about $24,000, and there is $10,000 of a revote. We are asking for a further amount of $18,000.

Toronto harbour is one of the most important harbours in Canada outside of a sea harbour. I suppose it is next to Montreal, if it is not ahead of Montreal. It is a work which is entirely under the control of the Dominion government. It has. without doubt, been neglected, and year after year damage is being done to the harbour and to the island, which, if not looked after now, will entail later on an expenditure of tens of thousands of dollars, where thousands of dollars will suffice now. The hon. minister knows that this year there has been exceptionally high water. Perhaps it is at high water mark in all our lakes. While I cannot speak from having visited the eastern end of the island this year, 1 can state, having visited the western end of the island, that the water is so high that the washing away of the island this year is more serious than it has been for ten years past. I think that in justice to' the important harbour of Toronto the hon. minister

should see that the matter is reported upon at once, and that a necessary amount is provided in the supplementary estimates to cover any expenditure that may be absolute ly necessary for this year. According to the statement in the * News ' there is only $18,000 available.
I will have to disclaim responsibility for the statements of the ' News,' there is $28,000 to expend.

Toronto harbour is so important that the government should not fail to grant sufficient money to keep it in proper condition. X am sure that the neglect of the government to expend a comparatively small sum of money immediately, would entail the expenditure of ten times as much in the future.

The minister (Mr. Hyman) is under a misapprehension when he says that one and a half million dollars have been spent on Toronto harbour by the government of this country. Not one single dollar has been spent by any government on Toronto harbour. The money he refers to has been spent upon the island and upon the canal through which vessels come into the harbour. Toronto harbour not only accommodates a great deal of commerce but it is a harbour of refuge as well, and some years
iigo it was consiuered good policy to have , channel built through the eastern end of the island. Some years ago the city of Toronto paid to the government $100,000 and were disenarged for all time to come from my obligation regarding that entrance. The government expenditure has been on works to prevent the washing away of the southern part of the island, and on that eastern entrance. The revenue derived from the shipping in the Toronto harbour has been devoted to improving the harbour from time to time by the harbour commissioners of Toronto, but I repeat that there never has been a dollar of public money expended upon the harbour itself. Three or four years ago the government appointed an engineer to consult with an engineer appointed by the city of Toronto in regard to the diversion of the Don, and the improvement of the harbour. The government engineer agieed with the engineer representing the city that certain works ought be carried out by the government, and the government, four years ago. put a sum of $7o,000 in the estimates but no money was spent. This appropriation was. put in the estimates for :he purpose of diverting the Don river which lows into the eastern end of the harbour and which river carries with it during the spring freshets, immense alluvial deposits from the surrounding country north and east, which have gradually filled np the beautiful harbour of Toronto which used, to have from fifteen to thirty feet ot water, but which now has only five or su fe t m certain places. The government have been appealed to by deputation after deputation. It was pointed out that the city of Toronto could in no sense be held responsible for the filling up the harbour by these alluvial deposits, and that the government should undertake the work of diverting the Don river to prevent this occurring. Within this last year or two the government has seen fit to drop that item from the estimates. Why. it is impossible for me to say ; after their own engineer reported in favour of this
___4 1,	4-	

under a moral obligation to the city of Toronto to go on with that work and save the harbour. I do not want the impression to
go forth that the government of Canada have spent public money on the Toronto harbour in any form, because it is not so.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Kemp) says he does not know why the government have dropped this item of $75,000 from the estimates, but he has been answered by his colleague (Mr. Osier) who said he agreed with the late Minister of Public W orks that there should be no expenditure on the harbour until the city took charge of the sewerage.
That was another item.

It was for the same work. 1 repeat what I said in answer to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) that I shall have the extension of the breakwater looked into immediately, and will provide, if there are further supplementary estimates, a sufficient amount to undertake that work.

I think there is more work required there. I understand that there has been considerable damage done west of- the breakwater on the eastern portion of the island, and that another year of high water and storm from the east may cause further material damage.
I will have the report of the hon. gentleman's remarks in ' Hansard *' with regard to that portion of the work, and the engineer will examine into it at the same time.

I wish to state that about a year ago the city council passed a resolution to the effect that they would accept responsibility for the sewerage, provided the government would do the work they had proposed to do according to the estimates submitted to parliament. So far as the city is concerned, I think it has relieved itself from any responsibility by passing that resolution. I would like to have it understood that these are two distinct questions. The question now before the committee is that of the breakwater at the eastern gap, for which the government is responsible, and for which the city of Toronto, by paying $100,000 some years ago, was relieved of responsibility. The other matter is one which we have been agitating for years ; and when money is being lavished on dredging, wharfs and other public works in small places all over the country, we do not understand how it is that the great city of Toronto, which has more freight to ship than any other place in this country, which ships much more freight than the city of Montreal, is so much neglected by the government. I would like the minister to tell us why the government neglects its duty in regard to the diversion of the Don in order that the deposits from that river may be diverted to Lake Ontario and not fill up the harbour in the future as it has done in the past.

I understand that it was only last year that the city council took Mr. KEMP.
this ground. So that whatever blame may be attached to the government could only be from last year.
It was previous to last session.

The government always took the stand that until the sewage was disposed of, it would be impossible for the government to do any work on the harbour. Personally I thoroughly appreciate the importance of the work and the importance of Toronto as a shipping point. I am only acting minister, but so far as I can, I will take pleasure in affording any expenditure possible to improve the shipping facilities at the port of Toronto ; and if the city council are prepared to enter into negotiations with the government for the disposal of the sewage in accordance with the plan laid down by the former Minister of Public Works, I shall be glad to take up the matter at any time.
Will the acting minister have any objection to reinstate in the supplementary estimates the sum which his predecessors committed themselves to for the straightening of the Don river V
I am not prepared to make that promise.
Wh/ was it taken out V

I think negotiations should first take place between the city and the government. It is a matter that would have to be discussed first departmentally and afterwards with my colleagues in the government.

I admit that. At the same time, the work need not be gone on with until a proper arrangement is come to with the city. The sum might be placed in the estimates conditional on such an arrange-met being made.

The only fear I have in regard to a matter of that kind is this. If we should put the $75,000 into the estimates and if by the end of, the year the government and the city were not able to come to any arrangement, I have no doubt that the government would be charged with having put it in for political purposes. Therefore I would not like to pledge myself, because I might get into trouble.

The $75,000 is only a drop in the bucket when the government are trying to find means of spending the tremendous surplus which they have; and, inasmuch as the hon. gentleman's predecessors committed themselves to this policy, I think he ought to be willing to reinstate the amount in the estimates, subject to a satisfactory arrangement being arrived at with the city of Toronto. In reference to the vote having a political tinge, the members from Toronto are willing to assume

any responsibility in that respect. I do not think the government need be afraid of being criticised for an expenditure of this kind in an important harbour like Toronto, in view of the tremendous amount of money being spent in Montreal, at Three Rivers, on the deep water wharf at Sorel, and on public works at other small places. If the minister reconsiders the matter, I think he will see that there is not much in that argument.

I presume that the hon. gentleman knows whereof he is speaking when he says that the city of Toronto passed such a resolution. Can he tell me whether it has been communicated to the Department of Public Works ?
Yes, and a deputation waited on the Minister of Public Works last year in reference to it. It was passed for the purpose of being communicated to the government.
Can the hon. gentleman remember the nature of the resolution-that the city desired to enter into negotiations with the government in regard to the matter ?
The city assumed all responsibility in regard to the sewage and the removal of it.

It would seem to me that the department would require something more than that, to guard against the harbour being filled up again with sewage. I think the hon. member should be satisfied with what I say, that I shall be glad to have the matter taken up immediately, with regard to reinserting the item in the estimates, I am not prepared to say off-hand that I will do so. I think the first item placed in the estimates was $75,000, and that in the following year $50,000 was inserted. I think it will be satisfactory if the minister will reinstate the sum of $50,000 in the supplementary estimates, subject to a satisfactory arrangement being arrived at with the city. If a satisfactory arrangement is not arrived at, then the amount drops.

If the minister would come up there himself, he could see the work that is required to be done. My colleague from East Toronto has stated the case correctly. Many years ago a celebrated engineer, Captain Eads, visited Toronto, and recommended the construction of a breakwater to separate Ashbridge bay from the harbour. That has not given satisfaction, for the reason stated by my hon. colleague. The freshets carry a large amount of alluvial matter down the Don river to the eastern part of the harbour.
The result is that there are scores of acres where the water is not more than two or three feet deep. The appropriation of $75,000 taken some years ago was intended, I think, to be expended in diverting the channel of the Don towards the southeast, so that the alluvial deposits would go to fill up Ashbridge's bay, which would be a great improvement. Instead of that, the debris flows into Toronto harbour, constantly filling it up.
The expenditures which have been made and which are charged against the Toronto harbour were incurred in order to protect the island, and in work on the eastern gap, As has been pointed out, on account of the water being so high in the lake, especially this year, great damage has been and is being done to the southern part of the island. But with regard to the harbour itself, there cannot be two opinions as to the necessity of a large expenditure being made to protect it ; and if the minister could find time to make a personal visit, he would be able to judge of the condition of the harbour for himself. As to the work of disposing of the sewage, that work is done by the city. There is a large quantity of sewage taken out of Toronto bay to-day at the expense of the corporation, which should be taken out at the expense of the government. As my hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) has pointed out, the sewage deposit is increased by the silt which is carried down by the river Don. The slips are continually being cleansed by the city dredges, and the engineer's estimates of the quantities dredged out would convince the hon. gentleman that the city of Toronto is not shirking in any way the obligation devolving upon it. This work of cleansing and deepening the harbour is necessitated by the action of the Don river, which has been declared a navigable stream, and over which the city of Toronto exercises no jurisdiction. Therefore the work of removing the silt brought down by the Don, which is being-performed by the city of Toronto, is not work the cost of doing which ought to be borne by that municipality. The government has expended a large sum in protecting the eastern end of the harbour, but that work will be practically of no value until steps are taken to remove from the harbour proper the accretions brought down by the river Don to the eastern end from year'to year. If the minister would read the report of his officers, endorsed by the report of Mr. Jennings, ho would see the reasonableness of the request made ; and no charge of political design on the city will be made against him if he will only comply with our reasonable request and put a substantial sum in the supplementaries to carry the desired work out. And if he should not be satisfied, after an examination and inspection, with the arrangement which the city of Toronto has made, then he heed

not spend a dollar. That proposition is so reasonable, coupled with the cordial invitation to the minister to come and see for himself, that I do not see how he can decline to come. The harbour is being steadily destroyed. Captain Bonicastle, fifty years ago, in prophetic words declared that that would be the inevitable result if the Don were allowed to continue pouring its flood into the harbour. The city undertook to pay the sum that was considered necessary and reasonable, namely the sum of $100,000, as its share of the work of preserving Toronto island. It provided that sum and handed it over to the Dominion. Inroads are being made on the island by the waters of Lake Ontario ; and it will not be argued that the municipality of Toronto is bound to protect an island two or three miles out in the lake from the depredations caused by the heavy storms from the east and south-east. The situation is a unique one. If the government desire to perserve the harbour, they must protect the island, and that can only be done as the result of an intelligent and systematic cooperation of the government with the municipality. A personal examination of the situation will convince my lion, friend that the statements of my colleague are absolutely within the mark and that it is necessary something should be done.

As regards the protection of the island, I would recommend strongly on my colleagues that a sufficient sum for the extension of the breakwater be put into any further supplementary estimates. With regard to the other question, I shall be glad to take the opportunity, either as acting Minister of Public Works or member of the cabinet, to visit Toronto and become acquainted with the whole work. The only advantage that I can conceive as having been accomplished has been the transfer of power from the control of the minister representing the province of Ontaro to that of a minister representing the province of Quebec, simply exploiting one department to give more patronage and more prestige to the minister of another department.
